basis: Ushojo manuẓo man clearly matches mánuṣa and the final-o man set. Its survey accent is explicitly INITIAL, unlike medial manúẓo in Gilgit and Palula. This is a counterexample to a pan-Shinaic root-final-before-o claim and must remain visible unless the primary transcription proves erroneous.
Ushojo ʌm mango matches āmrá after mr simplification; because mango terms circulate regionally, direct inheritance versus borrowing is not established by this short form. No accent is marked.

Ushojo laalo many matches the Shina lao/bahura many set, but the initial l and doubled l morphology need independent historical explanation. Initial stress and long first vowel are explicit; retain as a provisional lexical-family link, not a strict bahura sound law.
Ushojo mɔɔs meat matches māṁsá with long rounded vowel and final s. The survey gives no accent mark, so it contributes segmental quantity evidence but cannot confirm late-mora accent.
Ushojo dud milk is a short cluster-reduced dugdhá reflex. It is a control against assuming that every old cluster produces a modern long vowel, while its accent is unmarked.

Ushojo ẓembaṭh millstone is a mill-plus-stone compound comparable with Palula yan-baaṭ. The first member belongs to yantrá; baṭh belongs to the round-stone family11348. Compound-final stress is not the independent accent of the old yantra noun.

Ushojo mooz month matches mā́sa and the regional z-final month set; it has explicit length but no tone/stress mark. Its near-contrast with mɔɔs meat cannot establish the expected old barytone/oxytone accent difference without tone evidence.

Brokskat gun and Ushojo yun moon match the jyótsnā/yūn moon family, with Brokskat g corresponding to the palatalized onset. Both are unmarked in these records; modern quantity differs or is incompletely transcribed.

Ushojo loceki morning exactly matches the Shina loceki formation grouped under ruṣṭa. The added eki and medial stress belong to this extended temporal expression; the precise ruṣṭa versus ruc light-root ancestry remains open.
Ushojo phuti mosquito directly matches Palula phutti in the phutta small/insignificant insect family. It is independent of maśaka/matsara; initial stress is explicit and the short root is retained.

Ushojo maali mother pairs morphologically with maalo father and matches the mahallaka old-person kinship family. Initial syllable stress occurs in both; feminine i is a grammatical distinction, not evidence for mātṛ as the immediate ancestor.

Brokskat aae mother plausibly continues the āryikā/āje maternal term through medial consonant loss. The unequal ae sequence and possible expressive/contact origin leave this less secure than the maali family; retain as a candidate only.

Brokskat muumo maternal uncle matches the expressive māma kinship base with final o. Its initial stress is explicit despite a duplicated apostrophe in the stored spelling; it is not the longer mātula formation unchanged.
Brokskat ṣaṣ mother-in-law preserves the two sibilants of śvaśrū with strong contraction, matching Shina šaṣ. The short unmarked outcome does not test old final accent retention.

Ushojo khon mountain matches the khan/khoṇ terrain family currently split between khaṇḍa and skandha. This records that modern lexical connection but does not choose the contested old etymology from accent; source transcription has no marked accent.

Brokskat mauzi mouse/rat matches mūṣa with a voiced sibilant and final i. The written au may require source correction or diphthong interpretation; initial syllable stress is observable without assigning early/late mora.

Brokskat uzi mouth matches āsyà through vowel change and sy-to-z, comparable with Shina āzi. Initial stress is explicit, but the old svarita headword must not be relabeled unaccented or assigned an acute position.
Ushojo phuŋge moustache matches the phuṅga set in both consonants and plural e morphology. No accent is marked in this token.
Ushojo noom name matches nā́man after final syllable loss, with explicit long oo but no marked tone. It is an old-long barytone candidate with an unobserved accent outcome.
Ushojo thuni navel plausibly matches tundi/ṭuṅ navel rather than nābhi, with final feminine i. The aspiration and n/d reduction need regional confirmation; initial stress is explicit.

Brokskat grii neck is directly comparable with the older Brokskat grī already linked to grīvā́. The modern source lacks an accent mark, so it adds an attestation but not an independent tone confirmation.
Ushojo sũ needle matches sūcī through c loss and contraction; nasalization remains a regional development. Its unmarked single nucleus cannot identify the old final-accent reflex.
Brokskat nyy and Ushojo noo/nou new match náva after v loss or vocalization. The Ushojo alternatives differ in sequence/length notation, and neither source supplies a usable mora contrast.

Brokskat raat and Ushojo ṛaati night match the rātri/rātra set; final i is independently present in Ushojo and initial stress is explicit there. Brokskat's final-vowel loss does not distinguish old rātri from rātra, so the broad night family is used with that uncertainty.

Ushojo naõ nine clearly matches náva with v loss; Brokskat stored nur is the source's nine item but its r looks transcriptionally suspect and needs the printed vowel/nasal reading. Family identity is secure numerically; exact segmental or accent inference is deferred for Brokskat.
Ushojo anbiš nineteen transparently has subtractive ūna plus twenty, matching Palula aṇabhiiš; stress is on the twenty component. It belongs to a compound numeral class, not simple náva nine.

Brokskat nuto and Ushojo noti nose preserve the n/t frame of nasta with gender/final-vowel differences. Both have initial syllable stress; vowel quantity and the o/i cell distinction must remain separate.
Ushojo tɛl oil matches tailá with ai monophthongization; it is short and unmarked, so it cannot settle conflicting early/late readings in Gilgit long teel.

Ushojo puroono old preserves a three-syllable purāṇa formation and stresses the medial long root syllable before final o. It supports the root-final adjective class, while the earlier manuẓo initial-stress counterexample remains unresolved.

Brokskat jaaro old person matches jára with long first vowel and final o adjective/person ending. Initial stress is explicit; its lexical replacement of purāṇa must not be counted as a different reflex of that input.
Brokskat ek and Ushojo ɛɛk one match éka after final vowel loss; Ushojo marks length but no accent. Both belong to the independent one family, not a numeral analogy constructed from outcomes.

Ushojo palan onion matches palāṇḍú through cluster reduction and final vowel loss, but has explicitly INITIAL stress, unlike Palula palóṇ. This is a meaningful cross-language difference, not automatically resolved by attraction to the historically long medial vowel.
Ushojo tale palm matches tala flat surface/palm with final e and initial stress, independently distinct from the Kalkoti sthavira-derived hand term.
Brokskat pon and Ushojo pooṇ path match pánthā with cluster simplification and nasal retention. Ushojo marks length but no accent; no late/early classification is manufactured from the old headword.
Ushojo aro peach matches āḍu and regional āru through retroflex stop-to-flap change; final o and initial stress are explicit. Borrowing versus inheritance of the fruit name remains open.

Brokskat mus person plausibly continues the contracted manuṣya/mānuṣa set represented by Shina muš, rather than the uncontracted manuẓo formation. This segmentally motivated branch distinction is provisional between9828 and10049, and no accent is marked.
Brokskat hal plough matches halá and is a short unmarked counterpart to Palula haál. It cannot itself confirm the western late-mora pattern but preserves the h-conditioned lexical class.
Ushojo thun post/pillar matches sthū́ṇā with cluster simplification and final nasal, short or without transcribed length. No accent is marked.
